bull.b: Strong top-line growth combined with an exceptionally high gross-margin profile supports durable earnings power. The licensing and royalty model allows incremental adoption to scale without matching manufacturing investment, helping preserve profitability as Arm expands across computing markets.

Very low leverage gives Arm substantial financial flexibility to fund research, ecosystem development and new silicon initiatives without depending heavily on borrowing. A strong equity base also improves resilience if semiconductor cycles weaken or strategic investments take longer to mature.

Accelerating adoption in data centers and AI infrastructure broadens Arm beyond its established mobile position. Rising demand for energy-efficient compute, together with the AGI CPU pipeline, can support future licensing, royalty and silicon revenue growth across several structural workloads.

bear.b: Smartphone softness remains a meaningful drag because handset royalties are tied to customer chip shipments. Higher component costs can pressure device volumes and delay design activity, limiting near-term royalty growth while Arm’s newer data-center and AI opportunities scale.

Supply constraints could prevent Arm from converting strong AGI CPU demand into production volume and royalty-bearing shipments. Because management identifies several capacity bottlenecks, the timing of revenue realization and expansion beyond the initial opportunity remains dependent on ecosystem supply growth.

Moving into production silicon introduces a lower-margin phase than Arm’s traditional IP economics. Until scale, product maturity and cost improvements lift margins toward the long-term target, AGI CPU growth could dilute the company’s overall margin profile and increase execution sensitivity.
